subsection: 7. Culture, religion and science: identities, the Synod of Thurles, the creative arts and science

notes.h: Catholic identity and the devotional revolution
notes.b: After Catholic Emancipation (1829) removed the main political barrier, the Church was free to expand and organise. From the 1840s Catholic practice became more disciplined and more uniform, a change the historian Emmet Larkin named the devotional revolution (in an article of 1972).
points: Church building expanded sharply after Emancipation, with new parish churches and cathedrals raised on money collected from the faithful, so the Church's growth was visible in every town and parish.

St Patrick's College, Maynooth (founded 1795) trained most of the clergy, and by mid-century the priests were better educated and under closer episcopal discipline, so each bishop could direct his priests far more firmly.

Religious orders and congregations (communities of nuns and brothers) grew, and they ran schools, hospitals and orphanages. Examples are the Christian Brothers (Edmund Rice began his school in Waterford in 1802), the Presentation Sisters (Nano Nagle, Cork), the Sisters of Mercy (Catherine McAuley, Dublin, 1831) and the Sisters of Charity.

Parish missions, which were short, intense series of sermons given by Redemptorists, Vincentians and Jesuits, spread new forms of piety. These included the rosary, novenas (nine days of prayer), confraternities (lay prayer societies), benediction and devotion to the Sacred Heart and the Virgin Mary.

Larkin argued that weekly Mass attendance rose from about a third of Catholics before the Famine to a large majority (around 90 per cent) by the 1870s. Treat this as his claim, because other historians give a higher pre-Famine figure and argue that the change began earlier.

Historians link the change to the Famine (1845 to about 1850), which killed and removed the poor who had been least regular in practice, so those who remained were more observant. It also left a more prosperous farmer class and strengthened clerical authority.
The debate is whether the change was imposed from above by the clergy or grew from below.

Catholic identity became tied to nationality, because the Church's building programme and schools made it the main institution of the Catholic majority, who had been poor and shut out of power under the Penal Laws.
notes.tip: Define the devotional revolution in a sentence and attribute the Mass attendance figures to Larkin with 'about', since historians dispute them. Do not confuse it with Romanisation (Roman liturgy and ties) or ultramontanism (belief in papal authority).

notes.h: Protestant identity: evangelicalism, the Second Reformation and the Orange Order
notes.b: Protestants were a minority, and they responded to Catholic revival in two ways. Some pursued evangelical revival and conversion, while others defended Protestant privilege and loyalty to the Union. The result was sectarianism, meaning hostility between religious communities that shaped politics and everyday life.
points: Evangelicalism was a Protestant revival stressing personal conversion, Bible reading and missionary work. It grew in the Church of Ireland and among Presbyterians and Methodists from the 1820s.

The Second Reformation was the evangelical drive of the 1820s to 1850s to convert Catholics, using Bible societies, schools and missions. The name suggests a second attempt to spread Protestantism after the sixteenth-century Reformation.
Edward Nangle's mission colony on Achill Island (1834) and the Irish Church Missions (founded 1849 by Alexander Dallas) were well-known examples of this conversion drive.

In the Famine years, Protestant soup kitchens that required conversion led Catholics to coin the term souperism, meaning buying converts with food. The bitterness lasted for generations because it seemed to exploit starving people.

The Orange Order, founded in 1795, was dissolved in 1836 and revived in the 1840s. It expressed Protestant loyalty to the Crown, the Union and Protestant ascendancy (the dominance of Protestants in Irish life).

Henry Cooke, a Presbyterian minister and Ulster evangelical, promoted an alliance of Presbyterians and Anglicans against O'Connell and Catholic nationalism. This joined two Protestant groups that had often been rivals.
A great evangelical revival swept Ulster in 1859, which shows that Protestant revival continued strongly into the 1850s.

The Church of Ireland remained the established church (the state-backed church) until the Irish Church Act of 1869 took effect on 1 January 1871, although it served only a small minority of the population.
notes.tip: Keep the three terms apart: evangelicalism is the Protestant revival, the Second Reformation is the conversion drive, and souperism is the Catholic charge made during the Famine. Cover Protestant as well as Catholic identity, because a one-sided Catholic answer is limited.

notes.h: The nation, cultural nationalism and the decline of the Irish language
notes.b: Young Ireland, the group of nationalists around the newspaper The Nation, tried to define what the Irish nation was in terms of culture and history rather than religion. Yet while they praised the Irish past, the Irish language was in steep decline.
points: Young Ireland's idea of the nation was a community of shared history, culture and territory, so it could include Protestants as well as Catholics. This was meant to rise above sectarianism.
The Nation, founded in October 1842 by Thomas Davis, Charles Gavan Duffy and John Blake Dillon, used poems, ballads and history to teach this idea to ordinary readers.
Cultural nationalism in the 1840s encouraged the study of Irish history, manuscripts and antiquities (the remains and records of the past), but it did not stop the language declining.
O'Connell, though a native Irish speaker from Kerry, saw English as the language of progress, and had little interest in saving Irish.

The 1851 census, the first to record Irish speakers, found about 1.5 million, nearly a quarter of the population, reporting that they spoke it, so the language was still widely spoken despite its decline.
Irish was strongest in the west and south-west, where the Famine killed or scattered the poorest and the most Irish-speaking, so the heartland of the language lost people fastest.
The national schools, set up in 1831, taught through English, and parents saw English as the key to a job or to emigration, so many chose not to pass Irish on to their children.
notes.tip: For a short question on 'nation', define it as Young Ireland did (shared history, culture and territory, open to Protestants and Catholics) and give The Nation as the Irish example. For the language, name the 1851 census, the regional pattern and the parents' choice.

notes.b: Cullen was the architect of the Romanisation of the Irish Church and the leading Catholic figure of the period. Romanisation meant bringing the Irish Church into line with Rome, and he drove it as a direct participant.
points: Born near Ballitore, County Kildare, on 27 April 1803, he studied in Rome, was ordained there in 1829 and became rector of the Irish College in Rome in 1832.

Career: Archbishop of Armagh (appointed December 1849, installed early 1850), Apostolic Delegate (the pope's representative with special powers) in 1850, Archbishop of Dublin in 1852, first Irish cardinal in 1866; he died on 24 October 1878. He presided at the Synod of Thurles in 1850.

As a direct participant he drove the devotional revolution: ultramontane devotion (loyalty to the pope), strict clerical discipline, church building, religious orders, parish missions and Catholic schools. He opposed the Queen's Colleges and backed the Catholic University founded under Newman in 1854.

In politics he distrusted Young Ireland, the Tenant League (a farmers' organisation for tenant rights) and priests in politics, because he thought agitation threatened the Church's discipline. He also opposed the Fenians, a revolutionary movement.

In 1861 he refused to let the body of Terence Bellew MacManus, a Young Irelander who died in San Francisco, lie in the Pro-Cathedral in Dublin, which showed his hostility to revolutionary nationalism.
He favoured co-operation with the Liberals, and he supported Gladstone's Liberals. He did not oppose disestablishment of the Church of Ireland.
He shaped events but was also shaped by them. The Famine-weakened Church and Rome's backing gave him his chance, while MacHale's resistance and the failure of the Catholic University limited him.

Contemporaries differed. Supporters admired his devotion to Rome and his organisation, but nationalists and some bishops, notably MacHale, resented his authority. Historians see him as the central figure of the devotional revolution but debate whether he shaped Catholic political conservatism or reflected what the Church wanted.
notes.tip: The commonest essay asks about Cullen's influence on political attitudes and religious practice. Separate the two. Under religious practice put the Synod, Romanisation, devotions, discipline, orders and missions. Under political attitudes put his distrust of Young Ireland and the Fenians, priests out of politics and support for the Liberals. Give dated examples and state your judgement at the start.

notes.h: Case study: the Synod of Thurles, 1850 - background and causes
notes.b: A synod is a formal meeting of a Church's bishops. The Synod of Thurles was called to unify an Irish Church that had run its dioceses independently for decades and to settle the education question.
points: It was the first national synod of the Irish Catholic Church for about two centuries, the last having been held at Kilkenny in 1642, which is why it was seen as a landmark. Do not confuse the two synods.
Before 1850 each bishop ran his own diocese with little central direction, so clerical discipline and practice varied widely from place to place.

Rome wanted uniform practice and a clear Irish policy. Pope Pius IX also wanted the Church to resist the secular and mixed (non-denominational) education of the Queen's Colleges, the university colleges set up in 1845 at Belfast, Cork and Galway and opened in 1849.
The bishops were divided. John MacHale, Archbishop of Tuam, opposed the colleges outright, while Daniel Murray, Archbishop of Dublin (he died in 1852), was more willing to accept them.

A papal rescript (an official reply from Rome, here from Propaganda Fide) of 1847 had condemned the Queen's Colleges. The Famine had also weakened the old order and made Church leaders open to reform.
Rome made Paul Cullen Archbishop of Armagh in December 1849 and Apostolic Delegate in 1850, so that he could organise the Synod and carry out Roman policy.
notes.tip: Short answers ask why the Synod was held. Give two reasons: to unify the Church and to resist the Queen's Colleges. Keep MacHale (opponent), Murray (moderate) and Cullen apart.

notes.h: Case study: the Synod of Thurles - proceedings and decrees
notes.b: The Synod met in Thurles, County Tipperary, from 22 August to 9 September 1850. Its decrees (binding rulings) aimed to give the Church one policy on education, worship and discipline.
points: Cullen presided as Apostolic Delegate, so the meeting carried the pope's authority, and the bishops of the four provinces attended.
The decrees condemned the Queen's Colleges as dangerous to faith and morals and forbade clergy to take posts in them, because mixed education was seen as a threat to Catholic belief.
It ordered the setting up of a Catholic University, which opened in Dublin in 1854 with John Henry Newman as rector, so that Catholics would have an acceptable alternative.
It laid down uniform liturgical practice (the form of worship) and church discipline, with the Roman rite followed everywhere.
It regulated clerical dress, behaviour and the conduct of the sacraments, and increased the bishops' authority over priests.
It discouraged priests from political agitation, notably at the altar and election meetings, so the pulpit would not be used for politics.
Opposition came from MacHale and from lay Catholics and liberal clergy, who supported the Queen's Colleges and resented Roman control.
Rome supported Cullen, and the Synod's decrees were later confirmed there.
notes.tip: For short answers give when (22 August to 9 September 1850), where (Thurles, County Tipperary), who presided (Cullen) and two decrees, such as the condemnation of the Queen's Colleges and the Catholic University. Strong answers add a result.

notes.h: Case study: the Synod of Thurles - outcomes and significance
notes.b: The Synod began the Romanisation of the Irish Church and shaped Catholic life and politics for the rest of the century. Its education policy, however, met with limited success.
points: Ultramontanism was the belief in strong papal authority over national churches and bishops, and the Synod made it the guiding principle of Irish Catholicism.

Romanisation meant closer links with Rome, uniform liturgy and devotions in the Roman style, and a centralised Church under the bishops. It is related to, but not the same as, ultramontanism and the devotional revolution.
The Catholic University failed to attract many students and had no state-recognised degrees.
Most Catholics who wished to attend university still entered Trinity College or the Queen's Colleges, and the bishops later campaigned for a Catholic university with state support.
Cullen's authority over the bishops made him the dominant Catholic voice in public affairs for the next quarter-century, because he could speak for a united hierarchy.
Contemporaries disagreed. Protestants and some liberal Catholics saw an alien and authoritarian power, while supporters saw order and renewal.
Historians such as Emmet Larkin treat the Synod as the start of the devotional revolution, while others argue that the changes were already under way.
notes.tip: Examiners reward views as pairs: Protestants and liberal Catholics against papal control, against supporters' renewal; Larkin against historians who see earlier change. Give one result of the Synod, such as the Catholic University or Cullen's dominance.

notes.b: Aikenhead founded the Religious Sisters of Charity, an early Irish order of nuns devoted to work among the poor outside the convent. She was a participant, as founder, in the growth of Catholic social services.
points: Born in Cork on 19 January 1787 to a Protestant father and a Catholic mother, she became a Catholic.

Guided by Archbishop Daniel Murray of Dublin, she trained with the Bar Convent in York and founded the Religious Sisters of Charity in 1815. Do not confuse her with Catherine McAuley, who founded the Sisters of Mercy in 1831.
The Sisters visited the poor in their homes, ran schools and nursed the sick, which took nuns out of the enclosed convent and into the community.
In 1834 she opened St Vincent's Hospital in St Stephen's Green, Dublin, described as the first hospital in Ireland run by nuns, which treated the sick poor regardless of creed.
She directed the order from Stanhope Street in Dublin, the mother house, much of the time as an invalid, until her death on 22 July 1858.
As founder she was a participant in the growth of Catholic social services, not merely a witness, because she created the institutions herself.
Contemporaries admired her charity and her courage in running an institution while an invalid, for example in managing St Vincent's Hospital.
Historians see her as a pioneer of active women's religious life and Catholic nursing and as a founder of institutions that shaped Irish health care.
notes.tip: Do not call her order simply 'the first' to work with the poor, as the Presentation Sisters and Sisters of Mercy also did. Say an early one, or described as the first devoted to work outside the convent. For a paragraph on her give Cork 1787, Sisters of Charity 1815 and St Vincent's 1834.

notes.b: Carleton was the leading chronicler of the Irish peasantry before the Famine. He was a witness to the world he described rather than a political actor.
points: Born in 1794 at Prillisk, County Tyrone, the son of a Catholic Irish-speaking tenant farmer, he went to Dublin in about 1817 and began writing. He died in 1869.
He first wrote for the Christian Examiner, an evangelical Protestant paper, so his early stories had an anti-Catholic edge.
Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry appeared in 1830, with a second series in 1833, describing wakes, pilgrimages, faction fights and hedge schools (informal open-air schools).
Fardorougha the Miser (1839) and The Black Prophet (1847), a novel of famine, explored the life of the rural poor.
As a witness rather than a political actor, he recorded rural life without leading a movement. He received a government pension in 1848.
Contemporaries admired his realism, but some Catholic nationalists resented his early anti-Catholic writing.
Historians value him as a source on pre-Famine rural life and as a realist who showed the violence and poverty as well as the humour.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Carleton, the Tyrone novelist, with Kickham, the Fenian novelist. For a paragraph name the place (Prillisk), the dates and at least two works.

notes.h: Key personality: Thomas Davis and cultural nationalism
notes.b: Davis shaped the cultural idea of the Irish nation. Here only his cultural role is covered;
points: Born in Mallow in 1814 into a Protestant family, he was educated at Trinity College Dublin and called to the bar in 1838. In 1842 he co-founded The Nation with Charles Gavan Duffy and John Blake Dillon.
His songs and ballads, including A Nation Once Again and The West's Asleep, put history and patriotism into popular verse, so that people who did not read history could still learn it.
He urged the study and teaching of Irish history and the Irish language.
He argued that the nation should unite Catholic, Protestant and Dissenter (a Protestant outside the Church of Ireland) on a shared Irish identity.
He died of scarlet fever on 16 September 1845, aged 30, so his career was very short.
Contemporaries saw him as a model of principled youth, but critics thought his ideas were idealistic.
Historians credit him with laying the cultural foundations of Irish nationalism, though his appeal to Protestants was limited.
notes.tip: Davis was a Protestant of Mallow and belonged to Young Ireland, not the Fenians, and was not a Catholic like O'Connell. For a paragraph give Mallow, The Nation, his ballads and his death in 1845.

notes.h: The creative arts: literature, music, painting and antiquarian scholarship
notes.b: Irish writers, musicians and antiquarians (scholars of the past) drew on Irish history and folklore. Their work showed that Irish culture could win recognition even in a poor, divided country.
points: Thomas Moore's Irish Melodies, published in numbers from 1808 to 1834, set Irish airs to words and were popular in Britain, Ireland and America.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) wrote poems for The Nation, including Dark Rosaleen (1846), adapted from the Irish. He died of cholera in June 1849, in the Famine years.

George Petrie, painter and antiquarian, showed in an essay (of 1833, published in 1845 as The Ecclesiastical Architecture of Ireland) that the round towers were Christian in origin, and he collected traditional music in The Ancient Music of Ireland (1855).

The Ordnance Survey (the official mapping of Ireland) in the 1820s and 1830s employed scholars in its topographical department under Larcom's organisation. John O'Donovan and Eugene O'Curry recorded Irish place names and studied manuscripts, working with Petrie.
O'Donovan edited the Annals of the Four Masters (1848-51), and O'Curry became professor of Irish history and archaeology at the Catholic University (1854).
The Royal Irish Academy (1785) and the Royal Dublin Society (1731) supported scholarship.
The Famine drew writers to themes of hunger, eviction and emigration, as in Carleton's The Black Prophet.
notes.tip: A question on arts and science needs at least three named contributors, each with a work and a date (for example Moore, Mangan, Carleton, Petrie, O'Donovan, O'Curry), and a comment on what they showed about Irish culture despite poverty. A bare list earns little. Do not confuse Moore (Irish Melodies) with Mangan (poet in The Nation).

notes.b: Irish scientists made international contributions in mathematics, physics and astronomy, often in difficult conditions. This showed Irish capacity despite poverty.
points: William Rowan Hamilton, Royal Astronomer of Ireland at Dunsink, discovered quaternions (a kind of number used to describe rotations in three dimensions) on 16 October 1843 while walking by the Royal Canal at Broom Bridge, Dublin.

William Parsons, 3rd Earl of Rosse, built a six-foot reflecting telescope (one that gathers light with a mirror) at Birr Castle, known as the Leviathan. Completed in 1845, it was the largest in the world until 1917.
With it he saw the spiral shape of the galaxy M51, later known as the Whirlpool Galaxy, in 1845.
Nicholas Callan, a priest and professor of natural philosophy at Maynooth, built an induction coil in 1836 (a device that produces high voltage from a low-voltage current) and developed batteries.
George Boole was the first professor of mathematics at Queen's College Cork, from 1849, and published The Laws of Thought (1854), the basis of Boolean algebra, a way of handling logic.
Robert Kane, a chemist and first president of Queen's College Cork, wrote The Industrial Resources of Ireland (1844), urging the use of science for economic development.
The Queen's Colleges, the Royal Dublin Society and the Royal Irish Academy supported such work.
notes.tip: Name each scientist with an achievement and a date, such as Hamilton (quaternions, 1843), Rosse (the Leviathan, 1845), Callan (induction coil, 1836) and Boole (The Laws of Thought, 1854), and say what they showed about Irish ability.

notes.b: Judgements turn on whether the changes were imposed from above or grew from below. Examiners reward paired points that set achievements against limits and contemporary views against later ones.
points: Achievement of the devotional revolution: a more disciplined clergy, more churches and schools, and a strong Catholic identity, because the Church was now organised across the whole country.
Limit: the Church's authoritarian leadership split bishops, alienated liberal Catholics and Protestants, and left the Catholic University weak, so its gains were uneven.
Contemporary view: Protestants saw papal domination, while supporters saw renewal after the Famine.

Later view: historians broadly agree that the Church's changes gave Catholics a shared religious identity that later nationalism drew on. Larkin saw a revolution from the 1840s, while others argue that the change began earlier and grew from below.
Achievement of the arts and sciences: Moore, Carleton, Petrie, O'Donovan, Hamilton, Rosse and Boole won international recognition.
Limit: the Famine and emigration weakened the rural culture and the Irish language that cultural nationalists wished to save, because they removed the people who spoke and sang it.
notes.tip: Start an essay with a judgement and support it with dated examples. Cover Catholic and Protestant identity and the Young Ireland nation, with sectarianism as the link, since a one-sided Catholic answer is limited.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine and movement that stressed the authority of the pope over national churches and local bishops, which guided Cullen's reforms.
A Protestant revival movement stressing personal conversion, Bible reading and missionary work, strong among Irish Protestants from the 1820s.
A community bound by shared history, culture and territory, which Young Ireland used to define Irish nationality.
Hostility between religious communities, which shaped Irish politics, public processions and urban life.
The 1850 national synod of the Irish Catholic bishops under Cullen, which condemned the Queen's Colleges and reformed Church discipline.
The change in Irish Catholic practice after the Famine toward regular Mass, new devotions and closer clerical discipline.
The process by which the Irish Catholic Church adopted Roman liturgy and closer links with Rome and the pope.
The evangelical Protestant drive of the 1820s to 1850s to convert Irish Catholics through missions, schools and Bible societies.
The charge, made by Catholics, that Protestant relief agencies in the Famine gave food in return for conversion.
The pope's special representative, a title Cullen held in Ireland from 1850.
The belief that a nation is defined by its language, history, music and literature, promoted by The Nation.

factCards.term: Synod of Thurles: date and place
factCards.definition: Held at Thurles, County Tipperary, from 22 August to 9 September 1850, the first national synod for about two centuries.
It condemned the Queen's Colleges, ordered a Catholic University, and set uniform worship and clerical discipline.
Rector of the Irish College in Rome in 1832, Archbishop of Armagh in 1849, Archbishop of Dublin in 1852 and cardinal in 1866.
He condemned Fenianism and refused to let MacManus's coffin lie in the Pro-Cathedral in 1861.
He ran the Synod of Thurles, organised the Catholic University and drove the devotional revolution.
Founded by Mary Aikenhead in Dublin in 1815 to care for the poor in their homes, schools and hospitals.
Opened by Aikenhead's Sisters of Charity in St Stephen's Green, Dublin, the first Irish hospital run by nuns.
Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry (1830, 1833), Fardorougha the Miser (1839) and The Black Prophet (1847).
Protestant co-founder of The Nation in 1842, writer of A Nation Once Again, died of scarlet fever in 1845 aged 30.
Songs set to Irish airs, published in numbers from 1808 to 1834 and popular in Britain and America.
William Rowan Hamilton discovered quaternions on 16 October 1843 at Broom Bridge, Dublin.
A six-foot reflecting telescope built by Lord Rosse at Birr Castle, completed in 1845, and then the largest in the world.
First professor of mathematics at Queen's College Cork from 1849, author of The Laws of Thought (1854).
John O'Donovan and Eugene O'Curry recorded place names and manuscripts in the 1830s and 1840s.
A mass Protestant religious revival in Ulster in 1859.
